subject: ventures/terraform-plan-secret-exposure-check
professional: a senior DevSecOps / platform engineer who owns the Terraform CI pipeline and would wire `node cli.mjs check plan.json` in front of every apply; first checks: does it read the plan JSON exactly as Terraform writes it (internal/command/jsonplan, the JSON output format doc), does it respect every sensitivity marker Terraform emits (resources and outputs), does it cover every section of the plan file that carries values, and is the threat model it describes (what is and is not redacted where) accurate

evidence.correctness: Sources the author did not write, fetched for this audit: HashiCorp's JSON output format doc (web-unified-docs v1.13.x internals/json-format.mdx: before_sensitive/after_sensitive lines 621-627, output_changes uses the change representation, variables lines 121-128, prior_state line 76) and Terraform's own serializer internal/command/jsonplan/plan.go (lines 771-792: for output_changes 'BeforeSensitive and AfterSensitive will be identical, and either false or true'; there is no `sensitive` key on an output change; `sensitive` exists only on planned_values outputs, plan.go:185), plus `terraform show` docs (show.mdx:18: 'When using the -json command-line flag, any sensitive values ... will be displayed in plain text'). 15 hand-built plans run through engine.checkPlan (probe.mjs) and the CLI. Right: nested block lists with array-shaped after_sensitive mirrors (p3), a block collapsed to `true` (p10), module/indexed addresses and dotted map keys (p14), a GCP service-account JSON string with `BEGIN PRIVATE KEY` (p9), update shows before and after (p13), delete with before_sensitive (p15), 10 false-positive probes (AMI, sha256, UUID, ARN, git::ssh module source, registry:port image, mailto, host:port URL) all clean (p11). Wrong: an output declared `sensitive = true`, in the shape Terraform actually writes (after_sensitive:true, no `sensitive` key), is flagged and the CLI exits 1 (p1); `redis://:password@host` (empty user, the standard Redis AUTH URL) is missed (p8); values in prior_state, variables, configuration constant_value and resource_drift are never scanned (p4-p7, all 0 findings).
evidence.completeness: Claimed features checked: CLI human output and --json, exit 1 on findings / 0 clean / 2 on bad input (run), parse errors for non-JSON and missing resource_changes (engine tests), redaction to first/last four, browser page with file load, paste and worked example (served index.html loads engine.mjs/usage.mjs from the same origin, served engine.mjs byte-identical to source), the four docs/comparison pages (served, 307 to extensionless then 200), llms.txt and sitemap served. Usage tracking present: record('check_run'|'file_loaded'|'example_loaded') at index.html:160,172,204, DNT/GPC honoured (usage.mjs:34), opt-out button. Disclaimer ('No warranty ... not security, legal, or compliance advice') on the served page. No TODOs or dead links found. The one claimed sub-feature that does not work end to end is respecting output sensitivity (counted under correctness).
evidence.verification: `node --test '*.test.mjs'` in the subject root: 50 tests, 50 pass, 0 fail, 0.15 s. Five mutants via platform/ci/quality_mutate.py: 1 caught (dropping the output `sensitive` skip), 4 survived: pathIsSensitive's collapse-to-true short-circuit (engine.mjs:97) can be inverted with every test green, so a collapsed sensitive block is untested; the PEM header with no key-type word (`BEGIN PRIVATE KEY`, PKCS#8, the most common form) can be removed; the AWS key regex can be loosened to {12,} with no word boundary; redaction width change survives. The output-sensitivity test (engine.test.mjs:123) and the page's worked example (index.html:197) both use an invented `sensitive` key on output_changes, so the suite pins the wrong format and could not catch the false positive.
evidence.craft: Read engine.mjs (226 lines), cli.mjs (92), index.html script, usage.mjs, all four test files. Small, zero-dependency, one engine shared by page and CLI, redaction applied before anything is rendered, escapeHtml on output. Defects: the AWS pattern lists AIDA/AROA/AGPA/ANPA/ANVA/ASCA (IAM unique-ID prefixes, not access keys, and 21 characters long, so the alternation is dead and mislabelled) and omits nothing that matters; engine.mjs:149 is redundant with pathIsSensitive; CLI remediation text tells users to 'add sensitive = true to the attribute in the resource', which HCL does not allow (only variables and outputs take `sensitive`; elsewhere `sensitive()` wraps the expression).
evidence.claims: Checked: the docs page states 'terraform plan's human-readable output and the JSON from terraform show -json both replace the value with (sensitive value)' (why-terraform-plan-json-leaks-secrets.html:31, also on the served page): false per HashiCorp's show docs (show.mdx:18) and plan.go, the plan JSON carries every sensitive value in plaintext and only adds the *_sensitive maps. The same page lists a shared/committed plan JSON as an exposure surface the tool guards, so a clean report on a file full of plaintext sensitive values (fx/p_marked.json: password 'hunter2' in after, 0 findings, exit 0) reads as safe to share. vs-checkov.html:100 and vs-manually-reading...html:90 repeat 'a value Terraform already redacts'. 'outputs are sensitive as a whole, not per-path' is right in spirit but implemented against a key that does not exist. llms.txt:5 says 'Results are estimates from the numbers typed in, not legal, tax, financial ...' (calculator boilerplate, wrong for this tool). Issue numbers hashicorp/terraform#16554, #26185, #27577 could not be fetched through the proxy (403), so unverified, not counted against it. Scope (four patterns) and the no-guarantee disclaimer are stated plainly and accurately.
evidence.fitness: Job walked: generate plan, run CLI as a pre-apply gate. A config whose resources leak an unmarked key, PEM or credential URL is caught and blocks the apply with a redacted, pasteable report: that part works. But any root module that correctly declares `output "db_url" { sensitive = true }` holding a connection string (a very common pattern) fails the gate with advice to add the flag it already has, so the engineer must remove the gate or post-filter; and a team that follows the docs page's framing may share plan.json believing sensitive values are redacted in it.
evidence.domain: Compared against Terraform's JSON plan format and serializer: the resource-change walk follows the before_sensitive/after_sensitive contract correctly (collapse to `true`, arrays mirrored). Departures: output_changes sensitivity read from a non-existent field; the threat model conflates UI redaction with the plan file (which is itself a secret-bearing artifact a senior engineer would never share or log); the sections of the plan file that also carry values (prior_state incl. data sources read at plan, variables, configuration constants, resource_drift, which the human plan prints under 'Objects have changed outside of Terraform') are not scanned; Redis-style empty-user credential URLs missed. Pattern set is deliberately narrow and says so, which a practitioner would accept with Gitleaks alongside.

mutations.change: if (node === true) return true; -> if (node === true) return false;

defects.what: checkOutputChange reads `outputChange.sensitive`, a key Terraform never writes on output_changes (plan.go:771-792 emits before_sensitive/after_sensitive booleans). Every correctly declared `sensitive = true` output holding a URL with credentials, key or JWT is reported as unmarked and the CI gate exits 1, with advice to add the flag it already has. Repro: output_changes {db_url:{after:'postgres://admin:S3cretPw@db:5432/app',before_sensitive:true,after_sensitive:true}} -> 1 finding, exit 1. Fix: skip a side when outputChange[`${side}_sensitive`] === true (keep `|| outputChange.sensitive` for back-compat).

The docs page says `terraform show -json` replaces sensitive values with '(sensitive value)'; HashiCorp's show docs say -json output shows them in plain text, and the plan JSON always carries them. The page also lists a shared or committed plan JSON as an exposure the tool guards, so a clean report reads as 'safe to share' on a file holding every sensitive secret in plaintext.
The test for output sensitivity and the worked example use the invented `sensitive` key on output_changes, so the suite pins the wrong format instead of Terraform's.

Only resource_changes and output_changes are walked; resource_drift (printed by the human plan under 'Objects have changed outside of Terraform'), prior_state (incl. data sources read at plan time), variables and configuration constant_value are never scanned, though all carry plaintext values in the file.
Four of five seeded mutants survive: the collapse-to-true short-circuit in pathIsSensitive, the PKCS#8 'BEGIN PRIVATE KEY' form, the AWS key length/word boundary, and redaction width are untested.
URL credential pattern requires a non-empty username, so `redis://:password@host` (the standard Redis AUTH URL form) is missed.
CLI remediation tells users to add `sensitive = true` to a resource attribute; HCL accepts `sensitive` only on variable and output blocks (resource arguments need the sensitive() function).

AWS key pattern includes IAM unique-ID prefixes (AIDA, AROA, AGPA, ANPA, ANVA, ASCA) labelled 'AWS access key ID'; real unique IDs are 21 characters so the alternatives never match and only mislead a reader.
llms.txt carries calculator boilerplate ('Results are estimates from the numbers typed in, not legal, tax, financial ...') that does not describe a secret checker.

verdict: A small, clean, zero-dependency checker whose resource walk follows Terraform's before_sensitive/after_sensitive contract correctly (nested lists, collapsed blocks, module addresses, 10 false-positive probes clean, 50 tests green). It misses the bar on correctness, verification and claims: it reads output sensitivity from a field Terraform does not write, so every correctly marked sensitive output holding a credential URL, key or JWT fails the CI gate (plan.go:771-792; repro fx/p1.json, exit 1), and the tests and worked example pin that invented format. Its docs page also states that `terraform show -json` redacts sensitive values, the opposite of HashiCorp's documentation, inside a page that names a shared plan JSON as an exposure the tool guards. Four of five seeded mutants survive, and resource_drift, prior_state, variables and configuration are not scanned. The output fix is a one-line change; the docs line should say plan JSON always holds sensitive values in plaintext.
